**A larger batch changes both gradient noise and update frequency.** If an epoch contains a fixed number of examples, multiplying batch size by k produces roughly k times fewer optimizer updates per epoch. Simply changing the batch therefore changes the optimization trajectory even before any learning-rate adjustment. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

**Why linear scaling is a useful SGD heuristic.** When gradients change slowly over several small-batch steps, one larger step with a suitably larger learning rate can approximate their combined effect. This motivates scaling SGD's rate with batch size in some regimes. The approximation weakens when gradients change rapidly, curvature matters, or batches become too large.

Square-root rules for adaptive methods arise under particular noise/optimization assumptions; they are not universal replacements valid for every Adam configuration. Scheduler units, moment estimates, weight decay, and total training budget also change the comparison.

**Warmup addresses the fragile beginning.** Early parameters and statistics may not support the large steady-state step size. Increasing the rate gradually can avoid an immediate unstable jump. Warmup does not make an arbitrarily large final rate safe.

Distinguish fixed epochs, fixed updates, fixed tokens, and fixed wall-clock budgets. Monitor loss and validation behavior after scaling, and keep local per-device batch versus global batch explicit. A recipe that worked at one scale should be treated as a starting hypothesis, not a mathematical guarantee of unchanged accuracy.

**Technical details and references.**

For SGD, $k$ small steps with similar gradients total roughly $-k\eta g$. Replacing them with one update from a batch $k$ times larger motivates learning rate $k\eta$. The approximation fails when parameters and gradients change substantially across those skipped steps. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

Square-root scaling for adaptive optimizers arises under particular stochastic-dynamics assumptions; it is not a universal Adam rule. Warmup limits unstable early updates while moment estimates and network statistics settle. Beyond a critical batch size, larger batches yield diminishing statistical efficiency and fewer updates per epoch.

Track global batch, accumulation, update count, schedule units, and gradient-noise behavior. Retune when scaling hardware; keeping the same number of epochs does not preserve the same optimization trajectory or training budget.
